claims.claim: In adults with leg pain, having no pain when seated and symptoms that improve on bending forward are the most useful single history features pointing to the clinical syndrome of lumbar spinal stenosis.
claims.supporting_passage: Four studies evaluating 741 patients were identified. [...] The most useful symptoms for increasing the likelihood of the clinical syndrome of LSS were having no pain when seated (LR, 7.4; 95% CI, 1.9-30), improvement of symptoms when bending forward (LR, 6.4; 95% CI, 4.1-9.9), the presence of bilateral buttock or leg pain (LR, 6.3; 95% CI, 3.1-13), and neurogenic claudication (LR, 3.7; 95% CI, 2.9-4.8). Absence of neurogenic claudication (LR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.17-0.31) decreased the likelihood of the diagnosis. A wide-based gait (LR, 13; 95% CI, 1.9-95) and abnormal Romberg test result (LR, 4.2; 95% CI, 1.4-13) increased the likelihood of the clinical syndrome of LSS. [...] Absence of pain when seated and improvement of symptoms when bending forward are the most useful individual findings.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults (mostly older; highest-quality study mean age 65) with lower limb pain in spine and primary care clinics / history and examination findings / expert diagnosis with imaging confirmation / diagnostic accuracy (likelihood ratios) / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a review of 4 studies (741 people with leg pain), two answers were the strongest single pointers towards spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back): no pain when sitting, and symptoms that ease on bending forward. Leg pain on walking that goes away when the person sits, or leans forward on a shopping trolley, points towards the spine.
claims.qualifications: Keep likelihood ratios out of lay text or describe them as 'strong pointers'; never 'X times more likely'. Estimates come mostly from specialist clinics and may be less accurate in primary care. Confidence interval for 'no pain when seated' is wide (1.9 to 30). No single feature confirms the diagnosis; it needs imaging as well.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Nadeau 2013 (C10-22-d) found that individual symptom attributes were only weakly valid for telling neurogenic from vascular claudication head to head; combinations of symptoms were more useful. The two studies compare against different alternatives (Suri: all other causes of leg pain; Nadeau: vascular claudication only).

claims.claim: Leg pain from the circulation (vascular claudication) is typically not eased by changes in posture such as bending forward, tends to come on after a more consistent walking distance, and when the clinical picture is uncertain it can be checked with ankle brachial pressure (ABI) or vascular imaging.
claims.supporting_passage: Vascular intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease in particular is often considered when leg pain occurs with walking. Unlike neurogenic claudication, vascular claudication is typically not improved by changes in posture such as lumbar flexion.The discomfort of vascular claudication may be more consistently reproducible with a specific distance and time of ambulation than neurogenic claudication.When the diagnosis is uncertain by clinical evaluation, it can be confirmed by diagnostic testing including ankle brachial indices (ABIs), duplex ultrasound, computed tomographic angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography.
claims.location: Full text, Differential Diagnosis of the Clinical Syndrome of LSS
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with walking-related leg pain / clinical features of vascular vs neurogenic claudication / descriptive clinical guidance (review text, referenced)
claims.safe_wording: Leg pain from narrowed arteries is usually not helped by bending forward, and it tends to come on after about the same walking distance each time. If the history leaves doubt, checking foot pulses and ankle blood pressure (ABI) helps sort it out.
claims.qualifications: This is descriptive text in the review (citing other sources), not a pooled accuracy estimate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Nadeau 2013 found pain relievers and pain location individually only weakly discriminating; the difference is a tendency, not a rule.

claims.claim: In patients with claudication, calf symptoms that ease on standing still strongly suggest a circulation cause, while buttock or thigh symptoms that start on standing alone, ease on sitting and are helped by leaning on a shopping trolley strongly suggest spinal stenosis; single features on their own are weak.
claims.supporting_passage: We studied 53 patients. The most sensitive symptom attribute to rule out LSS was the absence of "triggering of pain with standing alone" (sensitivity 0.97, NLR 0.050). Pain alleviators and symptom location data showed a weak clinical significance for LSS and PVD. Constellation of symptoms yielded the strongest associations: patients with a positive shopping cart sign whose symptoms were located above the knees, triggered with standing alone and relieved with sitting had a strong likelihood of neurogenic claudication (PLR 13). Patients with symptoms in the calf that were relieved with standing alone had a strong likelihood of vascular claudication (PLR 20.0). [...] The classic symptom attributes used to differentiate neurogenic from vascular claudication are at best weakly valid independently. However, certain constellation of symptoms are much more indicative of etiology.
claims.pico_timeframe: 53 patients with diagnosed LSS or peripheral vascular disease reporting claudication, Canada / 14 symptom questions / neurogenic vs vascular diagnosis / likelihood ratios / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a small study of 53 people with walking-related leg pain, calf pain that eased when the person simply stood still pointed strongly to the circulation. Pain above the knee that came on just from standing, eased on sitting and was helped by leaning on a shopping trolley pointed strongly to the spine. Any one of these features alone was a weak guide.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre study; likelihood ratios imprecise. Participants already had one diagnosis or the other; people with both conditions are not addressed. Keep figures out of lay posts; 'strong pointer' is the safe phrase.

claims.qualifications: Qualitative, small, one hospital, people already listed for surgery: describes beliefs, not how common they are, and does not show that the X-ray description caused the avoidance. Avoid causal wording ('the X-ray made them stop').

claims.claim: After surgery, pain on movement is usually much worse than pain at rest, yet many trials measure only one kind of pain or do not say which.
claims.supporting_passage: "Only 39% of trials measured MEP and 52% failed to identify pain outcome as pain at rest (PAR) or MEP. Temporal trending did not suggest that MEP measurement is becoming more frequent. Trials measuring both MEP and PAR suggest that MEP is 95-226% more intense than PAR in the first 3 postoperative days. Among trials measuring MEP, 38% did not specify the physical maneuver used to assess MEP. Five of 7 meta-analyses reviewed (71%) did not distinguish between PAR and MEP [...] This is an important problem because MEP is usually more severe than PAR; MEP exerts a more direct adverse impact on postsurgical functional recovery and several current and novel pain treatments differentially affect MEP vs PAR."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in postsurgical analgesic trials (thoracotomy, knee arthroplasty, hysterectomy) / movement-evoked pain vs pain at rest / first 3 postoperative days / review of trial methods
claims.safe_wording: After an operation, pain when moving is usually much worse than pain lying still. In surgical trials that measured both, pain on movement scored roughly 2 to 3 times higher in the first 3 days. Yet only about 4 in 10 trials measured pain on movement at all.
claims.qualifications: Evidence is from postsurgical trials (including knee replacement), not older people or ward practice specifically. '2 to 3 times' is derived from '95 to 226% more intense' (1.95 to 3.26 times) and refers to average scores in trials that measured both; if in doubt, say 'much worse'. Fractures are not specifically covered.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence found on the direction; magnitude varies by operation and movement tested.

claims.claim: Pain on movement is the measure researchers now prioritise because it better reflects functional recovery.
claims.supporting_passage: Srikandarajah 2011: "MEP exerts a more direct adverse impact on postsurgical functional recovery". He 2025/2026: "We prioritized pain during movement over pain at rest, as it better reflects functional recovery."
claims.pico_timeframe: Postsurgical pain research / choice of pain outcome / expert rationale
claims.safe_wording: Pain researchers now often put pain on movement first, because it is the pain that gets in the way of recovery.
claims.qualifications: These are authors' statements of rationale, not measured comparisons of the two scores against function. Avoid 'proves' or 'shows' language.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Corbett 2019 notes that validation studies linking movement-evoked pain to function are still needed.

numbers.meaning: He network meta-analysis size (knee and hip replacement)

claims.claim: In older adults with chronic low back pain, more pain after standard movement tasks was linked with worse disability and physical function.
claims.supporting_passage: "226 older adults with chronic LBP. [...] LBP intensity was collected before and after the repeated chair rise test, stair climbing test, and 6-minute walk test [...] Greater aggregated posttest MeP was independently associated with worse disability (b = 0.593, t = 2.913, P = .004), self-efficacy (b = -0.870, t = -3.110, P = .002), and physical function (b = -0.017, t = -2.007, P = .039). MeP change scores were not associated with any outcome (all P > .050)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 226 older adults with chronic low back pain, US laboratory / pain after chair rise, stairs and 6-minute walk / adjusted regression / disability, confidence, physical performance / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 226 older adults with long-term back pain, those who had more pain after standing up from a chair, climbing stairs and walking also had more disability and did less well on tests of physical function.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional association; does not show that movement pain causes disability. One way of scoring movement pain (the change from before to after) showed no link. Effect sizes small.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study found here compared resting and movement scores head to head against function in older people.

numbers.meaning: older adults with chronic low back pain

claims.claim: The most commonly used pain measures record pain at rest or recalled pain, which does not capture pain during movement; measuring movement-evoked pain has been slow to reach clinical care.
claims.supporting_passage: "With musculoskeletal pain, the primary driver is often pain experienced during physical activity, commonly referred to as movement-evoked pain []. Yet, the most common used pain measures assess either spontaneous pain or pain recalled through the lens of questionnaires () []. Assessment of spontaneous pain, that does not involve physical activity, cannot discern pain related to movement." and "Burgeoning research supports movement-evoked pain measurement [;;], yet it remains slow to translate to clinical care []."
claims.location: Full text, Introduction (empty brackets are stripped reference markers in the rendered PMC text)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with persistent musculoskeletal pain / pain measurement practice / narrative review
claims.safe_wording: A pain score taken while someone lies still does not tell you how much it hurts to stand, turn or walk. Asking about pain during those movements gives the missing information.
claims.qualifications: Narrative expert review; the point is logical as much as empirical.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: UK national guidelines on assessing pain in older people ask for assessment of how pain affects function and activities, and for observation of pain behaviour during movement or care in people who can't self-report reliably.
claims.supporting_passage: Section 15, United Kingdom (p i14): "Where pain is present, a detailed clinical assessment of the multidimensional aspects of pain should be undertaken including: • Sensory dimension: the nature, location and intensity of pain • Affective dimension: the emotional component and response to pain • Impact: on functioning at the level of activities and participation." and "In people with very severe impairment, and in situations where procedures might cause pain, an observational assessment of pain behaviour is additionally required." Glossary (p i4 to i5): "Checklist of Non-verbal Pain Indicators (CNPI) A summation score of pain behaviours at rest and on movement"; "Mobilization Observation Behaviour Intensity Dementia (MOBID) An observational tool for use in early morning by carers to assess pain behaviours on five movements". Section 10 (p i10): "Re-wording your question to elicit the presence of pain such as 'Do you hurt anywhere?' or 'What is stopping you from doing what you want to do?' can substantiate the presence or absence of pain."
claims.location: Full text (PDF via Undermind): Section 15 UK subsection, p i14; Glossary, p i4 to i5; Section 10, p i10
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people in UK care settings / pain assessment / guideline
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance on assessing pain in older people asks how pain affects what the person can do, and for people who can't easily describe their pain, to watch them during movement or care. A practical question it suggests: 'What is stopping you from doing what you want to do?'
claims.qualifications: The guidance does not explicitly require a separate 'pain on movement' score for every patient; recording pain at rest and on standing is the post's recommendation (judgement) built on this guidance and C10-21-a. Some UK text is the 2018 document's summary of earlier UK guidance.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported. Suri 2010 (full text) gives the likelihood ratios for no pain when seated and relief on bending forward, the vascular-claudication contrast (not eased by posture; ABI or vascular imaging when uncertain) and the frequent coexistence of conditions. Nadeau 2013 adds head-to-head vascular vs neurogenic features (calf pain easing on standing still points to circulation; shopping-trolley sign with relief on sitting points to the spine; single features weak). Uesugi 2012 quantifies coexistence (about 7 in 100 LSS patients had PAD, half undetected). Katz 2022 and Suri confirm clinical picture plus imaging. As the judge asked, the post must say both conditions often coexist so pulses or ABI are still checked, keep likelihood ratios as 'strong pointers' and never convert them to 'times more likely'.

Trial and review claims are supported (PRECISE abstract; Enke 2018 and Shanthanna 2017), and participant ages are now verified (mean 52 and 55; adults 18 or older; people with creatinine clearance below 60 ml/min excluded). Two parts of the candidate fail as worded: (1) the NICE NG59 'do not offer gabapentinoids for sciatica' recommendation is available only as a search extract (the opened Enke 2018 records that the 2016 version pointed to neuropathic pain guidance endorsing gabapentinoids); (2) 'dizziness and drowsiness raise the risk of falls in older people' is contested (Chaitoff 2025 found no increase in fall-related visits with gabapentin vs duloxetine; Oh 2024 found higher odds in people with cognitive impairment). Adverse-event counts (227 vs 124) are events, not people; use 68/106 vs 43/101.
candidates.revised_angle: Reading the evidence: in the main placebo-controlled trial (207 adults with sciatica, average age about 52 to 55, people with reduced kidney function excluded), pregabalin did not ease leg pain more than a dummy capsule at 8 weeks or 1 year, and about 64 in 100 on pregabalin had side effects against 43 in 100 on placebo, dizziness most often; pooled reviews agree for gabapentin and pregabalin in back pain and sciatica. The trial under-represented older people, so it gives no reason to expect benefit in them, and dizziness and drowsiness are side effects that should weigh more for someone already unsteady (judgement, not a falls finding). What to do instead: explanation, staying active, and review of existing prescriptions started for sciatica. Mention NICE's advice only if the NG59 page is opened and the wording confirmed; otherwise say 'the trial evidence does not support starting them for sciatica'. Keep separate from the gabapentinoid swelling cascade post.

candidates.reason: The candidate's headline 'about 1 in 5 had troublesome pain months to years later' rests on Beswick 2012, which is now superseded by the 2025 update from the same group (Cheng et al., 68 studies, nearly 600,000 people, mean age about 70): about 22 in 100 at 3 months, falling to about 13 in 100 at 1 year and 15 in 100 at 2 years, with low confidence and probable underestimation. The 'most people get good relief' counterweight is supported by Bourne 2010 (about 4 in 5 satisfied; satisfaction with pain relief 72% to 86% by activity; unmet expectations the strongest predictor of dissatisfaction). The NICE referral claim could not be verified and is not needed.
candidates.revised_angle: Weighing it up: knee replacement relieves pain for most people, but in the most recent review about 13 in 100 still had troublesome knee pain a year after the operation (about 22 in 100 at 3 months), and the authors think the true figure may be higher. Unmet expectations were the strongest predictor of dissatisfaction in a large Canadian survey, so ask before surgery: 'What are my chances of still having pain afterwards?' and 'What else could I try first?' Icon array: about 13 in 100 at 1 year (from Cheng 2025), not 1 in 5. Do not give the 2012 and 2025 figures side by side without explaining the difference; state that 'troublesome pain' was defined differently across studies.

candidates.reason: Discordance (Bedson 2008), the counterweight that worse X-ray changes do go with more pain within a person (Neogi 2009), the specialist guidance that imaging is not needed for typical presentations but helps with atypical features or other possible diagnoses (EULAR 2017) and the 'bone on bone' beliefs that lead people to set aside exercise (Bunzli 2019) are all supported. The NICE NG226 wording (age 45 or over, stiffness under 30 minutes) is available only as a search extract, so the candidate's attribution to NICE must change unless the NICE page is opened.
candidates.revised_angle: What gets counted: a knee X-ray is a poor guide to how much a particular person will hurt or what they can do (population studies find wide mismatch), though on average worse changes do go with more pain. European rheumatology guidance (EULAR 2017) says an X-ray is not needed to diagnose typical knee osteoarthritis; imaging helps when something is unusual or another cause is possible. People told their knee is 'bone on bone' often come to fear exercise, which is one of the treatments that helps. Question to ask instead of 'what does the X-ray show?': 'What can I do to keep this knee moving, and what should make us look again?' Attribute the no-routine-X-ray point to EULAR unless NICE NG226 is opened and confirmed; avoid causal claims from the qualitative study.

candidates.reason: Essential claims supported with wording limits: movement-evoked pain is usually much worse than rest pain after surgery and often goes unmeasured (Srikandarajah 2011); resting or recalled pain scores do not capture movement pain (Corbett 2019); in older adults with chronic back pain, more pain after standard movement tasks was linked with worse disability and function (Knox 2023, cross-sectional); UK guidance asks for the impact of pain on function and observation during movement or care in people with severe impairment (Schofield 2018). As the judge noted, most evidence is postsurgical in adults of all ages; the post should say so, cite Srikandarajah or Corbett for the function link as expert rationale rather than proof, and drop the unverified ANZCA reference. Recording a 'pain on standing' line beside 'pain at rest' before therapy is a recommendation (judgement) built on this evidence.
